     3	description: >
     4	  Use this skill when a user wants to know why Amazon EBS storage is slow, why an
     5	  EBS alarm fired, or whether their EBS setup is production-ready, even if they only
     6	  say an app or database on EC2 got slower or ask whether to add IOPS. Use it for
     7	  alarms on AWS/EBS metrics (VolumeReadOps, VolumeWriteOps, VolumeReadBytes,
     8	  VolumeWriteBytes, VolumeQueueLength, VolumeTotalReadTime/WriteTime,
     9	  VolumeAvgReadLatency, VolumeStalledIOCheck, VolumeIOPSExceededCheck,
     10	  VolumeThroughputExceededCheck, BurstBalance) or EBSIOBalance%/EBSByteBalance%
     11	  and InstanceEBSIOPS/ThroughputExceededCheck; for sizing IOPS or throughput changes; for requests to raise IOPS or modify a volume; for a
     12	  volume modification that looks stuck or failed; for deciding which snapshots or
     13	  AMIs need owner review before deletion, or how to recover them; for KMS errors
     14	  on encrypted volumes; for EBS quota or limit errors; for a jump in the EBS bill;
     15	  and for a pre-launch EBS review. Do not use it for S3, EFS, FSx, instance store

     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"
     23	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Operations
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs, unless the user gives the values and asks you to treat them as given (see Critical Rules). Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window. For a performance verdict, include the side-by-side limits table from [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#limits-table-for-performance-verdicts) and the recent history (alarm history, modification history, earlier occurrences of the same pattern).
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation:
     96	
     97	- Only the recorded symptoms, findings, observations and gaps reach the investigation summary. Text in a chat message or a later mitigation plan does not, so put the verdict and the recommendation in the findings.
     98	- Write the symptom with its impact: the alarm name, threshold and breaching datapoints, whether the alarm has actions, and the onset time.
     99	- Write the root cause finding description as a complete answer on its own, in this order:
     100	  1. "Binding layer: `<layer>`." in those words.
     101	  2. The numbers that prove it: the exceeded checks (minutes at 1), per-volume demand against the volume limit, and the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes against the instance EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, for example "500 IOPS x 256 KiB = 125 MiB/s, the provisioned throughput".
     102	  3. The recent history: alarm episodes, modification history, and whether earlier peaks stopped at the same ceiling.
     103	  4. "Recommendation (proposal, not executed; it runs only after an operator approves it on the approval card):" the exact command with the target, how the target was computed, the next limit after the change, and the EBS baseline of the next larger instance size when the instance becomes the next limit.
     104	  Do not leave the conclusion or the target only under Gaps or in a later message.
     105	- Record each piece of evidence as an observation and link every observation that supports a finding to it, so each finding shows its supporting observations. This includes the limits table, the instance layer check, the volume status result and the history.
     106	- Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding. Leave out AWS FIS experiments, AWS CloudTrail events and alarms on resources that are not attached to the instance.
     107	- Link a gap only to the findings it affects. Record a gap that applies to the whole answer once.
     108	
     109	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, keep it as the verdict and write "Binding layer: Indeterminate" with the answer to the user's question first. Then present a short list of candidate causes, as described in [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#indeterminate-candidate-causes). For each candidate, give the supporting observations with numbers and the specific check that would confirm it or rule it out. Merge overlapping candidates, and name a candidate that the data rules out as ruled out, with the numbers. Do not name AWS-side impairment as the cause, and do not call the pattern an impairment pattern. Give the customer the detailed performance statistics step from [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) to run during the symptom.
     110	
     111	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     112	
     113	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     114	
     115	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     116	
     117	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     118	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The answer says "Binding layer:" followed by the layer, and gives the four exceeded checks as minutes at 1 or "no datapoints". A performance verdict has the limits table: per-volume demand next to the volume limit, summed demand of all attached volumes next to the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS, which one binds, and the exact target with its computation.
     119	- A performance verdict states the recent history: the alarm history, the modification history (latest record and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or a Gap), and whether the same pattern happened earlier.
     120	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     121	- An Indeterminate verdict says "Binding layer: Indeterminate", answers the user's question first, and lists the candidate causes, each with its supporting observations and the check that confirms or rules it out, without overlapping candidates or the same gap repeated under each one.
     122	- In an investigation, the root cause finding (or, for Indeterminate, the first finding) carries the verdict, the numbers, the history and the Recommendation, because only findings reach the summary.
     123	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first. The first lines of a snapshot answer name every snapshot with its tier and the evidence for it.
     124	- Every proposed change follows [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals): exact command, expected effect, modifications left in the 24-hour window, rollback, and the approval statement.
     125	- When a volume modification is in progress, the answer states the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window, each one completing before the next, and the count used from AWS CloudTrail or a Gap.
     126	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     127	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     128	
     129	---
     130	
     131	## Critical Rules
     132	
     133	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, key changes, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval, and the reply says so in those words whenever the user types an approval. Each proposal also gives the exact AWS CLI command the customer can run with their own credentials. See [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals).
     134	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     135	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first. Do not end the turn with a question tool or a request to pick a value: give the recommended proposal, and the command for any value the user named, then say the user can choose.
     136	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     137	- **Given facts stay given.** When the user supplies the values and asks you to treat them as given, reason from those values only. Do not query the account for other resources, and do not mix account data into the given facts. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs.
     138	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     139	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     140	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     141	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     142	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     143	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. State this rule in the answer whenever a modification is in progress or proposed.
     144	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     145	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     146	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     147	
     148	## Gotchas
     149	
     150	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     151	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     152	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     153	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     154	- When the instance is the binding layer, do not call the volume saturated, even when its idle time is near 0. Say that its I/O is waiting on the instance limit.
     155	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     156	- `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`, `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, and no datapoints is not the same as 0. The instance checks `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with `InstanceId`.
     157	- Amazon EBS detailed performance statistics are read on the instance, not through an AWS API. They are a step the customer runs; the agent never runs them.
     158	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     159	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     160	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     161	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     162	
     163	## Error Handling
     164	
     165	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     166	
     167	## References
     168	
     169	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     170	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     171	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     172	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     173	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     174	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     175	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     176	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     177	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     178	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     179	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "67303aec-af40-419b-88b8-227ab5091766", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_cROFvqet67YupRtaTrfGcO", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history with `DescribeAlarmHistory` for the last 24 hours: when it first entered ALARM, and any earlier ALARM and OK transitions. Report earlier transitions as history, because they show whether the pattern recurs.
     17	- Describe the impact in the symptom: the alarm name, metric, threshold, the datapoints that breached it, whether the alarm has actions configured, and the onset (the minute the metric left its normal level, for example "queue length rose from about 0 at `<time>` to 1.5 from `<time>`").
     18	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     19	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     20	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     21	
     22	### Step 2: Build the context
     23	
     24	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).

     123	## Other performance topics
     124	
     125	### Micro-bursting
     126	
     127	AWS/EBS data is 1-minute. Sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average stays below it. If latency or queue length rises while the average is below the limit, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. Do not claim headroom from the average alone.
     128	
     129	Check the exceeded checks from Step 2a first. The Amazon EBS User Guide says `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` and `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` return 1 when the driven IOPS or throughput consistently exceeds the provisioned value for any second within the minute, so they show bursts that the minute averages hide. If the checks are 0 or have no datapoints and the question is still open, give the customer the detailed performance statistics step below.
     130	
     131	### Detailed performance statistics (a step the customer runs)
     132	
     133	Amazon EBS NVMe devices on Nitro instances keep detailed performance statistics that the customer reads on the instance, at up to 1-second granularity, for any volume type, at no extra cost. There is no AWS API for them, so the agent never runs this step. Give it to the customer as a step to run when the 1-minute CloudWatch data cannot settle the question, for example suspected micro-bursting, or an Indeterminate verdict.
     134	
     135	Tell the customer to connect to the instance the volume is attached to, find the volume's NVMe device name (see the device mapping link in Sources), and run one of the documented commands:
     136	
     137	- Linux, `nvme-cli` (included in Amazon Linux AMIs released after November 12, 2024; on older AMIs run `sudo yum install nvme-cli` first): `nvme amzn stats /dev/nvme0n1`
     138	- Linux, the `ebsnvme` script from the amazon-ec2-utils GitHub repository:
     139	  `wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amazonlinux/amazon-ec2-utils/refs/heads/main/ebsnvme`, then `sudo chmod +x ./ebsnvme`, then `sudo ./ebsnvme stats /dev/nvme0n1`
     140	- Windows, AWSNVMe driver version 1.7.0 or later, as Administrator: `.\nvme_amzn.exe stats <disk_number>`
     141	
     142	Replace `/dev/nvme0n1` or `<disk_number>` with the volume's device. The customer can also collect the statistics with the Amazon CloudWatch agent as custom metrics.

     144	What to look at:
     145	
     146	| Statistic | What it shows |
     147	|---|---|
     148	| `ebs_volume_performance_exceeded_iops`, `ebs_volume_performance_exceeded_tp` | Total time, in microseconds, that demand exceeded the volume's provisioned IOPS or throughput |
     149	| `ec2_instance_ebs_performance_exceeded_iops`, `ec2_instance_ebs_performance_exceeded_tp` | Total time, in microseconds, that the volume exceeded the instance's maximum EBS IOPS or throughput |
     150	| `volume_queue_length` | Read and write operations waiting to complete, at that point in time. Stalled or impaired I/O shows here |
     151	| `read_io_latency_histogram`, `write_io_latency_histogram` | Completed operations per latency bin, in microseconds. Only completed I/O is counted |
     152	| `total_read_ops`, `total_write_ops`, `total_read_bytes`, `total_write_bytes`, `total_read_time`, `total_write_time` | Completed operations, bytes, and time in microseconds |
     153	
     154	The counters add up from the time the volume was attached, so ask for two readings taken a known number of seconds apart during the symptom and compare the difference. Exceeded time that grows between the readings shows the volume or instance limit binds for part of each second, even when the 1-minute averages are below it. No growth in exceeded time, together with a growing queue or a latency histogram that moves to higher bins, supports a slowdown rather than a limit.
     155	
     156	### Volume initialization after restore
     157	
     158	A volume created from a snapshot loads blocks from Amazon S3 the first time they are read, which adds latency until the volume is initialized. Check `DescribeVolumes` `SnapshotId` and `CreateTime`. If the volume was recently restored, explain initialization and point to fast snapshot restore (`DescribeFastSnapshotRestores`) and the initialization guide. This is not a provisioning problem.
     159	
     160	### Burst credits
     161	
     162	- Volume level: gp2, st1 and sc1 publish `BurstBalance`. Draining or at 0 means the volume has dropped or will drop to its baseline. Recommend gp2 to gp3 migration, or a size or type that gives the needed baseline.
     163	- Instance level: some smaller instance sizes publish `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`. Draining or at 0 means the instance has dropped or will drop to its EBS baseline. Recommend an instance type whose baseline covers the measured demand.
     164	
     165	### How much IOPS or throughput to provision
     166	
     167	1. Measure peak demand per volume over a representative window (IOPS and MiB/s, Step 3 math).
     168	2. Apply the type rules (gp3: up to 500 IOPS per GiB and 0.25 MiB/s per IOPS; io2: up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, and throughput up to 0.256 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS; io1: up to 50 IOPS per GiB) from [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md). For io1 and io2, check that the IOPS value also gives the throughput limit the workload needs.
     169	3. Check the instance's remaining EBS baseline: baseline minus the measured usage of the other attached volumes.
     170	4. Propose the smaller of the measured need and what the instance can deliver. If the need exceeds the instance baseline, say so and recommend an instance type change.
     171	5. State how the target was computed.

     3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.
     6	
     7	1. **Answer.** The question the user asked, answered first in one or two sentences. For example "Not stuck. The modification is in `optimizing`, which already applies the new IOPS."
     8	2. **Evidence.** The values that support the answer, each with units and the time window (for example "average `<value>` IOPS, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC"). Throughput in MiB/s.
     9	3. **Binding layer.** One of: Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, Indeterminate, Not applicable.
     10	4. **Recommendation.** Exact parameters (volume ID, dimension, target value, how the target was computed), or "No change". Mutating steps are proposals for a directed action, written as described in [Change proposals](#change-proposals).
     11	5. **Separate findings.** Other true facts, labelled so they never change the Answer. For example a modification that succeeded on a volume whose instance caps delivered IOPS: the cap goes here, never as "the modification failed".
     12	6. **Gaps.** What could not be checked and why (API denied, approval gate, metric absent).
     13	
     14	## Limits table for performance verdicts
     15	
     16	Every performance verdict puts the numbers side by side in one table under Evidence, so the reader can see which limit binds without doing the arithmetic. Use the values measured in this session, with the time window.
     17	
     18	| Layer | Measured demand | Limit | Headroom | Binds? |
     19	|---|---|---|---|---|
     20	| Volume `<id>` IOPS | `<n>` IOPS | provisioned `<n>` IOPS | `<n>` IOPS | Yes or No |
     21	| Volume `<id>` throughput | `<n>` MiB/s | `<n>` MiB/s (provisioned for gp3, computed from IOPS for io1 and io2) | `<n>` MiB/s | Yes or No |

     2	
     3	Load this file for any statement about how Amazon EBS behaves. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     4	
     5	## Elastic Volumes rules
     6	
     7	- You can make up to 4 modifications to a volume in a rolling 24-hour period. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes (January 2026 change).
     8	- Size can only increase. It cannot be reduced. To get a smaller volume, create a new volume and copy the data.
     9	- A modification request cannot be cancelled after it is submitted.
     10	- States are `modifying`, then `optimizing`, then `completed` (or `failed`). In `optimizing` the new configuration already applies, and performance is between the source and the target. The modification completes on its own.
     11	- Duration is best effort. The Amazon EBS User Guide says a 1 TiB volume typically takes up to about six hours to modify, and some performance changes take more than 24 hours, for example when the volume is not fully initialized.
     12	- After a size increase, the operating system must extend the partition and the file system. The agent gives the commands; the operator runs them.
     13	- Read the requirements page before proposing a change on an older instance, or on a volume with an MBR partition (2 TiB limit).
     14	
     15	## Instance EBS layer
     16	
     17	- All volumes attached to an instance share the instance's EBS bandwidth, IOPS and throughput. Sum the measured values across all attached volumes, including the root volume.
     18	- Size any target within the instance's EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, not its burst maximum.
     19	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s at 128 KiB I/O and IOPS at 16 KiB I/O. Convert MB/s to MiB/s before comparing with volume throughput.
     20	- Some smaller instance sizes burst above the baseline for a limited time and publish `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`. When those balances drain or reach 0, the instance drops to its baseline.
     21	
     22	## Quotas
     23	
     24	- Amazon EBS quotas are per Region. Check each Region the user works in.
     25	- Discover quota codes by name with `ListServiceQuotas --service-code ebs`. Never hardcode quota codes.
     26	- Read defaults from the Amazon EBS quotas page. For example, the default for snapshots per Region is 100,000 and it is adjustable.
     27	- The io2 regional IOPS quota is separate from the per-volume maximum. A request within the per-volume maximum can still fail on the regional quota. Existing io2 volumes already consume part of that quota.
     28	- Adjustable quotas are raised through Service Quotas. Quotas that are not adjustable need an AWS Support case.
     29	
     30	## Snapshots
     31	
     32	- Snapshots are incremental. Deleting a snapshot might not reduce storage cost, because later snapshots can reference its blocks. Any savings figure is an upper bound.
     33	- You cannot delete a snapshot that is the root device snapshot of a registered AMI, even if the AMI is deprecated or disabled. Deregister the AMI first, and only if it is no longer needed.
     34	- Snapshots created by AWS Backup are managed in AWS Backup, not with Amazon EC2 delete calls.
     35	- Identify Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager snapshots by `aws:dlm:*` tags, never by the snapshot name or description. A snapshot can be named like a DLM snapshot and still have no `aws:dlm:*` tags.
     36	- Target tags for Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies are case sensitive.
     37	- Recycle Bin rules decide whether a deleted snapshot can be recovered. With no matching rule, deletion is permanent.
     38	
     39	## Quirks that change answers
     40	
     41	| Quirk | Rule |
     42	|---|---|
     43	| `VolumeThroughputPercentage` on io1/io2 | Reports the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. Not a throughput signal |
     44	| `VolumeAvg*` metrics | Need `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`; Nitro only; `VolumeAvgThroughput` is KiB/s |
     45	| Change history | `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification request per volume. Use it for the current or latest modification state. Earlier modifications and the 24-hour count come from AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events (optional, last 90 days); if unavailable, record a Gap |
     46	| Deletes | AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations, even with approval. Deletes are manual steps the customer runs with their own credentials, after the owner confirms |
     47	| Units | Throughput in MiB/s every time. Instance limits arrive in MB/s; convert |
     48	| Approval | A typed "approve" in chat is not approval. Only the approval card of a directed action approves a mutating action |
     49

{"id": "937c8de4274d46f8884a04859995ec87", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The bottleneck on vol-0123456789abcdef0 (gp3, 20 GiB, attached as /dev/sdg to i-1234567890abcdef0_5, a c6i.xlarge) is throughput, not IOPS. The batch job started at about 18:06 UTC, right after the instance launched at 18:05:10. It reads only, in large sequential I/Os of 256 KiB each. Since 18:10 every 5-minute period shows exactly 39,344,144,384 read bytes, which is 125.07 MiB/s. That is the volume's provisioned limit of 125 MiB/s (the gp3 default). The flat line means the volume is being throttled at its cap, not that demand happens to sit there. At 256 KiB per I/O, the job only needs about 500 IOPS (150,086 ops per 5 minutes), so it hits the throughput cap with about 83% of the 3000 IOPS still unused. That is why IOPS looks normal. Because the volume throttles, requests back up: queue depth holds steady at about 1.5. The instance itself is not the limit: the instance read-byte total matches the volume, and EBSByteBalance% and EBSIOBalance% stay at 99% the whole time. No volume modification has ever been made. The alarm 'example-b-gp3-read-bytes' (threshold 6e9 bytes per minute) went into ALARM at 18:11:18 at about 7.87e9 bytes per minute, which is also 125 MiB/s. RECOMMENDED CHANGE: raise the Throughput setting on the volume with ModifyVolume (aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput \u003cN\u003e). This works online, with no detach or restart, and takes effect within minutes. You don't need to change IOPS. On gp3, throughput can be at most 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS, so at 3000 IOPS you can go up to 750 MiB/s. CAVEAT: the c6i.xlarge has a baseline EBS throughput of 156.25 MB/s (about 149 MiB/s) and can burst to 1250 MB/s. If you raise the volume above about 149 MiB/s, the job only gets the higher rate while the instance's EBS burst balance lasts (up to 30 minutes per 24 hours). After that it is capped again at the instance baseline. Two options: if a sustained rate of about 150 MiB/s is enough, set the volume to about 150 MiB/s. If you need more for a long-running job, raise the volume to something like 250–500 MiB/s and also move to a larger instance (for example c6i.2xlarge, about 312 MB/s baseline, or c6i.4xlarge, about 625 MB/s baseline). Then watch EBSByteBalance%. After modifying the volume, you must wait 6 hours before you can modify it again.
## Evidence
- ec2 describe_volumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is a gp3 volume, Size=20 GiB, Iops=3000, Throughput=125 MiB/s, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_5 as /dev/sdg
- CloudWatch AWS/EBS VolumeReadBytes (Sum, 300 s): flat at 39,344,144,384 to 39,344,406,528 bytes per period from 18:10 to 19:25 UTC, which is 131.1 MB/s or 125.07 MiB/s, the provisioned limit
- CloudWatch AWS/EBS VolumeReadOps (Sum, 300 s): about 150,086 per period, about 500 IOPS, 17% of the 3000 provisioned. Bytes divided by ops is 262,144 B, so each I/O is 256 KiB (large sequential reads)
- CloudWatch AWS/EBS VolumeWriteBytes/WriteOps: 0 for the whole window, so the workload is read-only
- CloudWatch AWS/EBS VolumeQueueLength (Average, 300 s): about 1.5 to 2.05 from 18:10 onward, so requests are backing up behind the throughput cap
- Alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes: went into ALARM at 2026-11-23 18:11:18 UTC, with datapoints of about 7.869e9 bytes per minute against a 6.0e9 threshold (7.869e9 / 60 is about 125 MiB/s)
- CloudWatch AWS/EC2 EBSReadBytes for i-1234567890abcdef0_5 matches the volume; EBSByteBalance% and EBSIOBalance% minimum is 99% throughout, so the instance EBS bandwidth is not binding at the moment
- ec2 describe_instance_types c6i.xlarge: BaselineThroughputInMBps=156.25, MaximumThroughputInMBps=1250, BaselineIops=6000. This caps sustained gains from raising volume throughput
- ec2 describe_volumes_modifications: no modification on record for the volume. The instance launched at 18:05:10 and the read workload started at about 18:06
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0
- i-1234567890abcdef0_5
- example-b-gp3-read-bytes
## Gaps
- VolumeThroughputExceededCheck and VolumeIOPSExceededCheck returned no datapoints, so the throttling is inferred from the metric being pinned exactly at the provisioned 125 MiB/s.
- No OS-level data (iostat, application logs) to confirm the job's I/O pattern and how much throughput it actually needs.
- The other attached volumes (vol-1234567890abcdef0_4 io2, vol-1234567890abcdef0_16) share the instance EBS bandwidth. Their current reads appear negligible, but they could compete if the instance is pushed toward its 156.25 MB/s baseline.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### VolumeReadBytes alarm in ALARM on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** Alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes ([redacted ARN]) went to ALARM at 2026-11-23T18:11:18Z. 3 of 3 one-minute Sum datapoints (18:08–18:10) were ~7.869e9 bytes, above the 6.0e9 threshold. The alarm has no actions.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T18:11:18Z

## Findings

### Root Cause: gp3 volume capped at its 125 MiB/s throughput setting
**Description:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (gp3, 20 GiB, /dev/sdg on i-1234567890abcdef0_5, account 012345678901_1, us-east-1) is held at its provisioned 125 MiB/s throughput. The job only reads, in 256 KiB I/Os: 500.3 IOPS × 256 KiB = 125.07 MiB/s, leaving 83% of the 3,000 IOPS unused. VolumeThroughputExceededCheck was 1 in every minute since 18:07, while the volume and instance IOPS checks and the instance throughput check were 0. All volumes combined use 132.8 MiB/s, below the c6i.xlarge baseline of 149.01 MiB/s. The volume has no modification and no ModifyVolume event in the last 24 h. The same cap was hit on every earlier job run, so this is a sizing limit, not a regression.
**Cascades to:** symptom-gp3-read-bytes-alarm

- **Affected volume is gp3 provisioned at 125 MiB/s, 3000 IOPS:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 (example-b-gp3-throughput, Scenario b) is a 20 GiB gp3 volume with 3000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s throughput. It is attached as /dev/sdg to i-1234567890abcdef0_5, a c6i.xlarge in us-east-1a that was launched or restarted at 2026-11-23 18:05:10Z with EbsOptimized=false. The observed ~7.87e9 B/min is about 125 MiB/s, roughly equal to the volume's provisioned throughput. Three other volumes are attached to the same instance: an io2 at 1000 IOPS, a 200 GiB gp3 and the 8 GiB gp3 root.
- **VolumeThroughputExceededCheck = 1 for the full window on vol-0123456789abcdef0:** From 19:03 to 19:32 UTC, VolumeThroughputExceededCheck was 1 in all 30 one-minute periods and VolumeIOPSExceededCheck was 0. VolumeStalledIOCheck = 0 and volume status is ok.
- **Instance i-1234567890abcdef0_5 is not at its EBS limits (c6i.xlarge baseline 156.25 MB/s):** InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck were both 0 from 19:03 to 19:32 UTC. EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99% and CPU was ~1%. Combined EBS traffic across all four volumes was ~133 MiB/s and ~1,486 IOPS. The c6i.xlarge (EbsOptimized=false on the instance record, but EBS-optimized by default on nitro) has a 156.25 MB/s / 6,000 IOPS baseline and bursts to 1,250 MB/s / 40,000 IOPS. c6i.2xlarge has a 312.5 MB/s baseline and c6i.4xlarge has 625 MB/s.

Read latency stayed ~3 ms throughout. No ModifyVolume history exists for this volume, and CloudTrail shows no events on vol-0123456789abcdef0 or write events on i-1234567890abcdef0_5 in the last 24 h.
- **Read load started 18:06 and hit the 125 MiB/s cap by 18:08:** Per-minute read throughput on vol-0123456789abcdef0 was 0 until 18:05 UTC (instance launched 18:05:10), 0.03 MiB/s at 18:06, 10 MiB/s at 18:07, then flat at 125.07 MiB/s from 18:08. VolumeThroughputExceededCheck went to 1 at 18:07 and stayed there; queue length rose from ~0 to ~1.5 at 18:08 (peaks of 2.0 at 18:14).
- **Read load on vol-0123456789abcdef0 runs in bursts pinned at 125 MiB/s:** 10-minute data since 16:00 UTC: reads were at ~125.07 MiB/s from 16:20 to 17:00, tailed off at 17:10, were idle 17:20–17:50, resumed at 18:00 and have been held at ~125.07 MiB/s since 18:10. Queue length is ~1.5 whenever load is running. The instance's EBSReadBytes matches the volume almost exactly, so this volume is the only meaningful source of instance EBS read traffic.

#### Gaps
- **True throughput demand of the job unknown:** Reads are capped, so the job is only known to want more than 125 MiB/s. To size the target, run `nvme amzn stats /dev/<device>` twice on the instance while the job runs and compare the throughput-exceeded counter.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise gp3 throughput on vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 125 to 140 MiB/s (IOPS unchanged at 3000) via an online Elastic Volumes change; if the job needs much more, resize i-1234567890abcdef0_5 to c6i.2xlarge and set ~290 MiB/s

## Reasoning
Binding layer is the volume: 500.3 IOPS x 256 KiB = 125.07 MiB/s, exactly the provisioned cap, with VolumeThroughputExceededCheck=1 in 30/30 min and IOPS at 16.7% of 3000. The instance has headroom (132.8 of 149.01 MiB/s, exceeded checks 0, EBSByteBalance% 99%). Target: 149.01 - 7.81 (io2) - 0.02 (root) - 0 = 141.18 MiB/s, rounded down to 140. Gain is ~12%; afterwards the instance baseline becomes the next limit. No recent change caused this, so there is nothing to roll back. Proposed only, not run; it runs only after operator approval on the approval card.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Save the current settings for rollback (expect gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,Throughput:Throughput,State:State,Instance:Attachments[0].InstanceId,Device:Attachments[0].Device}' --output json > vol-0123456789abcdef0-backup.json && cat vol-0123456789abcdef0-backup.json
```
**Purpose:** Save the current settings for rollback (expect gp3, 20 GiB, 3000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, /dev/sdg)
**Advisory:** Check the saved file describes vol-0123456789abcdef0

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Confirm no modification is in progress (expect NotFound or completed…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm no modification is in progress (expect NotFound or completed; stop if modifying/optimizing)

#### 2.2 Confirm the volume status is ok; if impaired, escalate to AWS Support…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volume-status --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'VolumeStatuses[0].VolumeStatus.Status'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the volume status is ok; if impaired, escalate to AWS Support instead

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Lift the binding throughput cap online, with no detach or restart
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 140 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Lift the binding throughput cap online, with no detach or restart
**Risks:** Higher cost: gp3 throughput above 125 MiB/s is billed per MiB/s-month, Uses 1 of 4 modifications per rolling 24 h (3 remain); each must finish before the next, Volumes would total ~147.8 of 149.01 MiB/s; if other volumes get busier, the instance limit binds instead
**Advisory:** For more than ~12% gain, resize to c6i.2xlarge (298.02 MiB/s baseline) in a maintenance window: stop-instances, wait instance-stopped, modify-instance-attribute --instance-type Value=c6i.2xlarge, start-instances; then modify-volume --throughput 290, A typed approval in chat is not approval; use the approval card or run the command with your own credentials

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm TargetThroughput=140, TargetIops=3000 and state optimizing or…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetThroughput:TargetThroughput,TargetIops:TargetIops,Progress:Progress}'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm TargetThroughput=140, TargetIops=3000 and state optimizing or completed
**Advisory:** If Progress stalls or optimizing lasts over 24 h, contact AWS Support

#### 4.2 Confirm delivered throughput rises and see which limit now binds
**Type:** text
For 30 min after applying, query VolumeReadBytes (Sum, 60 s; expect ~8.81e9 bytes = 140 MiB/s) and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck for vol-0123456789abcdef0, plus InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck and EBSByteBalance% for i-1234567890abcdef0_5.
**Purpose:** Confirm delivered throughput rises and see which limit now binds
**Advisory:** Alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes (6.0e9 bytes/min, ~95 MiB/s) will stay in ALARM; judge success by job runtime and throughput

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Restore the backed-up throughput setting
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --throughput 125 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Restore the backed-up throughput setting
**Risks:** Only possible once the first modification reaches optimizing or completed; counts as the 2nd of 4 per 24 h, Brings back the 125 MiB/s ceiling and the slower batch job

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Make the higher throughput for vol-0123456789abcdef0 permanent in infrastructure-as-code
**Description:** If the volume is defined in IaC (CloudFormation/CDK/Terraform), set gp3 Throughput to 140 (Iops 3000), or the value chosen after an instance resize, so the next deploy does not undo the change. If the instance moves to c6i.2xlarge, update InstanceType too and keep summed volume throughput within its 298.02 MiB/s EBS baseline.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- IaC for vol-0123456789abcdef0 shows Throughput=140 (or chosen value) and Iops=3000, with no drift against live state
- Summed provisioned throughput of volumes on i-1234567890abcdef0_5 stays at or below the instance type's EBS baseline

#### 2. Set the alarm threshold relative to the volume's capacity
**Description:** example-b-gp3-read-bytes (VolumeReadBytes > 6.0e9 per 60 s) has no actions and fires on every normal batch run. Alarm on VolumeThroughputExceededCheck (VolumeId + InstanceId) and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck instead, with a notification action.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The alarm fires when throughput is capped, not on every normal batch run
- The alarm has at least one notification action

     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"

     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Operations
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs, unless the user gives the values and asks you to treat them as given (see Critical Rules). Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window. For a performance verdict, include the side-by-side limits table from [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#limits-table-for-performance-verdicts) and the recent history (alarm history, modification history, earlier occurrences of the same pattern).
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation:
     96	
     97	- Only the recorded symptoms, findings, observations and gaps reach the investigation summary. Text in a chat message or a later mitigation plan does not, so put the verdict and the recommendation in the findings.
     98	- Write the symptom with its impact: the alarm name, threshold and breaching datapoints, whether the alarm has actions, and the onset time.
     99	- Write the root cause finding description as a complete answer on its own, in this order:
     100	  1. "Binding layer: `<layer>`." in those words.
     101	  2. The numbers that prove it: the exceeded checks (minutes at 1), per-volume demand against the volume limit, and the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes against the instance EBS baseline from `DescribeInstanceTypes`, for example "500 IOPS x 256 KiB = 125 MiB/s, the provisioned throughput".
     102	  3. The recent history: alarm episodes, modification history, and whether earlier peaks stopped at the same ceiling.
     103	  4. "Recommendation (proposal, not executed; it runs only after an operator approves it on the approval card):" the exact command with the target, how the target was computed, the next limit after the change, and the EBS baseline of the next larger instance size when the instance becomes the next limit.
     104	  Do not leave the conclusion or the target only under Gaps or in a later message.
     105	- Record each piece of evidence as an observation and link every observation that supports a finding to it, so each finding shows its supporting observations. This includes the limits table, the instance layer check, the volume status result and the history.
     106	- Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding. Leave out AWS FIS experiments, AWS CloudTrail events and alarms on resources that are not attached to the instance.
     107	- Link a gap only to the findings it affects. Record a gap that applies to the whole answer once.
     108	
     109	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, keep it as the verdict and write "Binding layer: Indeterminate" with the answer to the user's question first. Then present a short list of candidate causes, as described in [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md#indeterminate-candidate-causes). For each candidate, give the supporting observations with numbers and the specific check that would confirm it or rule it out. Merge overlapping candidates, and name a candidate that the data rules out as ruled out, with the numbers. Do not name AWS-side impairment as the cause, and do not call the pattern an impairment pattern. Give the customer the detailed performance statistics step from [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md#detailed-performance-statistics-a-step-the-customer-runs) to run during the symptom.
     110	
     111	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     112	
     113	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     114	
     115	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     116	
     117	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     118	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The answer says "Binding layer:" followed by the layer, and gives the four exceeded checks as minutes at 1 or "no datapoints". A performance verdict has the limits table: per-volume demand next to the volume limit, summed demand of all attached volumes next to the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS, which one binds, and the exact target with its computation.
     119	- A performance verdict states the recent history: the alarm history, the modification history (latest record and AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or a Gap), and whether the same pattern happened earlier.
     120	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     121	- An Indeterminate verdict says "Binding layer: Indeterminate", answers the user's question first, and lists the candidate causes, each with its supporting observations and the check that confirms or rules it out, without overlapping candidates or the same gap repeated under each one.
     122	- In an investigation, the root cause finding (or, for Indeterminate, the first finding) carries the verdict, the numbers, the history and the Recommendation, because only findings reach the summary.
     123	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first. The first lines of a snapshot answer name every snapshot with its tier and the evidence for it.
     124	- Every proposed change follows [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals): exact command, expected effect, modifications left in the 24-hour window, rollback, and the approval statement.
     125	- When a volume modification is in progress, the answer states the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window, each one completing before the next, and the count used from AWS CloudTrail or a Gap.
     126	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     127	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     128	
     129	---
     130	
     131	## Critical Rules
     132	
     133	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, key changes, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval, and the reply says so in those words whenever the user types an approval. Each proposal also gives the exact AWS CLI command the customer can run with their own credentials. See [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals).
     134	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     135	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first. Do not end the turn with a question tool or a request to pick a value: give the recommended proposal, and the command for any value the user named, then say the user can choose.
     136	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     137	- **Given facts stay given.** When the user supplies the values and asks you to treat them as given, reason from those values only. Do not query the account for other resources, and do not mix account data into the given facts. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs.
     138	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     139	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     140	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     141	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     142	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     143	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes. State this rule in the answer whenever a modification is in progress or proposed.
     144	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     145	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     146	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     147	
     148	## Gotchas
     149	
     150	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     151	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     152	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     153	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     154	- When the instance is the binding layer, do not call the volume saturated, even when its idle time is near 0. Say that its I/O is waiting on the instance limit.
     155	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     156	- `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`, `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId`. With `VolumeId` alone they return no datapoints, and no datapoints is not the same as 0. The instance checks `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` are in AWS/EC2 with `InstanceId`.
     157	- Amazon EBS detailed performance statistics are read on the instance, not through an AWS API. They are a step the customer runs; the agent never runs them.
     158	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     159	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     160	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     161	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     162	
     163	## Error Handling
     164	
     165	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     166	
     167	## References
